bio.en: Andy Johns is a former legendary growth leader at Facebook, Twitter, Quora, and Wealthfront who left a path to CEO to become a mental-health advocate helping burned-out high achievers and veterans.
bio.zh: Andy Johns 曾是 Facebook、Twitter、Quora 和 Wealthfront 的传奇增长负责人，他放弃了成为 CEO 的职业路径，转而成为心理健康倡导者，帮助精疲力竭的高成就者和退伍军人。

summary.en: Andy shares his personal story of burnout and transformation, explaining the physical and behavioral signals—sleep, relationships, health—that act as flashing red alarms for wellbeing. He lays out a four-step process for making lasting change and how to actually allow that change to happen in your life. The conversation is a candid, real-talk episode on mental health, burnout, and reclaiming your path in and beyond tech.
summary.zh: Andy 分享了自己倦怠与转变的个人故事，讲解了睡眠、人际关系、健康等作为身心健康“红色警报”的生理与行为信号。他给出了实现持久改变的四步法，以及如何真正让改变在自己身上发生。这期对话坦诚直白，聚焦心理健康、倦怠，以及在科技行业内外重新找回人生方向。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: There are day-to-day stresses that are normal and we just have to put up with, but then there's the other stuff that's the flashing red alarm. Again, you can go back to animals. It's like when their fundamental functions, when their core behaviors of diet, exercise, playfulness, socialization, sleep, when those things get disrupted, it's a sign that there is something going on here that you need to take a look at. (00:00:27): So the same is true with people. If your sleep always sucks, if your relationships are constantly strained or frequently strained, if your physical health is failing, there's so many ways that that can be measured. So there's really no excuse for that to say, "Oh, I just didn't know." I'd say it's to look at those things. When those are suffering or when they're really out of whack, it's undeniable that there is something that is detrimental to your wellbeing that's going on right now, and your body is telling you, "Stop. Something needs to change."
turns.zh: 有日常的压力是正常的，我们只能忍受；但还有另一种东西是闪烁的红色警报。同样，你可以回到动物身上——当它们的基本功能、核心行为——饮食、运动、玩耍、社交、睡眠——这些被打乱的时候，那就是一个信号，说明这里有什么事你需要看一看。(00:00:27)：人也是一样。如果你的睡眠总是很糟，如果你的人际关系经常或频繁地紧张，如果你的身体健康在恶化——有很多方式可以衡量这些。所以真的没有借口说'哦，我只是不知道'。我会说就看这些东西。当这些在受苦、真的失衡的时候，不可否认，有某种正在损害你幸福感的事情正在发生，你的身体在告诉你：'停下来，有些事需要改变。'

turns.zh: 好，就着这个话题，我很想让你讲讲你走过的路。基本上，你在某种意义上跟我一样——你帮公司做产品、驱动增长，跟世界上一些最好的公司合作过，然后事情发生了转折。你能简单概述一下发生了什么吗？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Sure. So the short background is I spent about 17 years working in the world of startups. I think on the whole, it was a successful experience. I managed to land at a handful of really good companies and had a great experience, but along the way, despite having built somewhat of an impressive resume, I guess you could say, I was also struggling quite a bit in terms of my emotional, psychological, and spiritual health. So in some ways, it feels like the cliche that as my career reached its pinnacle, that from a professional, from a financial perspective, I was at my highest, but when it came to other aspects of my life, I was arguably at my lowest or close to my lowest. (00:06:43): So even though I had those successes, there was a lot that I needed to work through that was under the hood, which I eventually came to understand very, very deeply as a result of turning inward and doing a lot of work on my own path towards self-understanding and healing some deep emotional wounds.
turns.zh: 当然。简短的背景是我在创业公司世界里工作了大约 17 年。总的来说，这是一段成功的经历。我有幸进入了几家非常好的公司，体验很棒。但一路走来，尽管我建立了某种程度上令人印象深刻的简历，可以说吧，我在情感、心理和精神健康方面也挣扎得相当厉害。所以在某些方面，感觉就像那个老套的故事——当我的职业生涯达到顶峰，从专业、从财务角度我处于最高点，但在生活的其他方面，我可以说是处于最低点或接近最低点。(00:06:43)：所以即使有那些成功，也有很多我需要处理的东西藏在表象之下，我最终通过转向内在、在自己通往自我理解和疗愈深层情感创伤的道路上做了大量工作，才非常非常深刻地理解了这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In a post that you worked on for my newsletter back in the day, you shared this story of, I think maybe it was at Wealthfront where you were giving a big presentation. Maybe share that story?
turns.zh: 在你当年为我 newsletter 写的一篇文章里，你分享了一个故事，我觉得可能是在 Wealthfront，你在做一个大型演讲。也许讲讲那个故事？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Sure. I can share that. It actually goes back to ... This is 2010. I was at Twitter at the time. I was in my late 20s. Again, my career was going really well. I was starting to string together a series of successful experiences, and I was suddenly hit with near constant panic, panic attacks, depression. I was having a very, very difficult time sleeping and just managing my emotions as a whole. It got to the point to where there were several occasions while I was at work where I could tell that I was about ready to have a breakdown of sorts, and I would just grab my laptop, throw it in my bag, and pretty quietly just walk out of the office even if it was 10:00 AM and I'd only been there for an hour or two. That happened on multiple occasions. (00:08:07): There were some occasions in which I was set up to go and speak to the entire company during an all-hands session, and it was something where I just had to come up with an excuse and bow out of it because at the time, I was already completely overcome and overwhelmed by this near constant panic I was experiencing, but I had a really good poker face, I don't think most people could see it. (00:08:34): To give a little bit of an explanation and to tie first question together with this, there were two major things that contributed to me having a pretty acute case of burnout and needing to step away from my career as I knew it. The first was just the slow and steady accumulation of the pressure, the stresses, the anxieties, the emotional ups and downs that came from having such a strong commitment to my career, and frankly an addiction to achievement as a way to feel good and to feel whole, but I was so focused on my work that I had slowly become the frog that was boiling in the pot, the typical analogy of you don't realize how bad things are getting because it's happening to you slowly until it happens quickly, right? (00:09:38): So on one hand, I was not only struggling emotionally and psychologically because of the pressures of the career and climbing the ladder and just the common existential angst that comes with being at a startup and not knowing what the future holds. What I later came to understand was that I was also starting to experience and to address old emotional pain that I'd buried for a very long time, stemming back to the death of my mom when I was 10. She was severely mentally ill. She was bipolar, had bouts of psychosis, and had spent time in and out of psychiatric hospitals. I can remember going to those hospitals as some of my earliest memories as a kid. (00:10:33): So there was a lot of disruption in my childhood, a lot of neglect, some occasional abuse, and then it culminated with the loss of the most important female figure in my life when I was 10. Of course, like anyone else after that, I was in a lot of pain emotionally, but as a kid, you don't have the tools or even the capabilities to effectively process something as significant and traumatic as an experience like that. (00:11:11): So my mind did what the mind of most children will do, which is it finds a way to bury it or to ignore it. The thing that I had latched onto that made me feel better was that anytime I hit a home run or scored a goal or got straight A's and was just basically a stellar student and a stellar athlete, I was showered with love, not only from my family, which is fantastic, but from society at large, especially within the world that we live in. (00:11:44): So I learned very early on that if I wanted to feel good, I needed to achieve, and that if I wanted to love myself and be considered lovable by others, I needed to achieve. That pulled me out of a darkness that I was in for several years as a kid, and I'm glad that it did, and it led to an excellent experience in high school, in college, and then well into my 20s, but eventually, those emotional wounds are going to come to the surface. They're going to come up for error, and when they do, it's going to be difficult, and that's what happened with me. (00:12:24): So it was really two things coming together at the same time. It was the growing pressures of an escalating career within the dynamic industry, but then also, I think, the natural maturation of my mind and of adult development such that it was time for that old pain to come to the surface, and when it did, it was very disruptive and it's something that I'm still continuing to work on to this day.
turns.zh: 好的，我可以分享。其实要追溯到……那是 2010 年，我当时在 Twitter。我快 30 岁。同样，我的职业生涯进展顺利，我开始一连串地积累成功经验，然后我突然被近乎持续的恐慌、恐慌发作、抑郁击中。我睡眠非常非常困难，整体上很难管理自己的情绪。到了这个地步——好几次在公司里，我能感觉到自己快要崩溃了，我就抓起笔记本塞进包里，然后相当安静地直接走出办公室，即使才上午 10 点、我才到了一两个小时。这种事发生了好几次。(00:08:07)：有几次我被安排在全公司 all-hands 会议上讲话，但我不得不找个借口推掉，因为那时候我已经被这种近乎持续的恐慌完全压倒和淹没了，不过我的扑克脸很好，我不觉得大多数人能看出来。(00:08:34)：为了解释一下，也把第一个问题跟这个联系起来——有两件大事导致了我相当严重的倦怠，需要离开我所熟悉的职业生涯。第一件就是压力、焦虑、情绪起伏的缓慢而稳定的积累，这些来自于我对职业生涯的强烈投入，坦白说也来自于一种把成就当成感觉良好、感觉完整的成瘾方式。但我太专注于工作了，以至于我慢慢变成了那只锅里慢慢被煮沸的青蛙——那个典型的比喻，你没意识到事情变得多糟，因为它在慢慢发生在你身上，直到它突然变快，对吧？(00:09:38)：所以一方面，我不仅在情感和心理上因为职业压力、爬阶梯、以及在创业公司里不知道未来会怎样的那种常见存在主义焦虑而挣扎。我后来理解到的是，我也开始经历和处理我埋藏了很久的旧的情感痛苦——追溯到我妈去世的时候，我 10 岁。她有严重的精神疾病，她是双相情感障碍，有过精神病发作，进出过精神病院。我记得小时候去那些医院是我最早的记忆之一。(00:10:33)：所以我的童年有很多动荡、很多忽视、偶尔有虐待，然后在我 10 岁的时候以失去我生命中最重要的女性人物而告终。当然，像其他任何人一样，那之后我在情感上非常痛苦，但作为一个孩子，你没有工具、甚至没有能力去有效地处理像那样重大和创伤性的经历。(00:11:11)：所以我的心智做了大多数孩子的心智会做的事——它找到一种方式去埋藏或忽视它。我抓住的、让我感觉好一点的东西是——每次我打出本垒打、进球、拿全 A、基本上做一个出色的学生和出色的运动员时，我就会被爱包围——不仅来自我的家人，这很棒——还来自整个社会，特别是在我们生活的这个世界里。(00:11:44)：所以我非常早就学到了：如果我想感觉良好，我就需要去成就；如果我想爱自己、被别人认为是可爱的，我就需要去成就。那把我从孩子时期好几年的黑暗中拉了出来，我很高兴它做到了，它让我在高中、大学、一直到 20 多岁都有出色的体验。但最终，那些情感创伤会浮出水面，它们会冒出来要求被处理，当它们冒出来的时候，会很困难，这就是发生在我身上的事。(00:12:24)：所以真的是两件事同时发生：一方面是一个在不断升级的行业里 escalat ing 职业的越来越大的压力，另一方面我认为是我的心智和成人发展的自然成熟，到了让那些旧痛苦浮出水面的时候，当它浮出水面时，它非常 disruptive，是我至今仍在继续处理的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people listening either resonate with some of this or just like, "This is exactly the life I'm living." I know you work with people now helping them through these challenges, especially in tech. So two questions there. One is just you've done polls around this. Just what percentage of people in tech have you seen struggle with these sorts of things on some degree?
turns.zh: 我猜很多听众要么对此有共鸣，要么觉得'这正是我正在过的生活'。我知道你现在跟人合作，帮他们度过这些挑战，尤其是在科技行业。所以有两个问题。一是你做过相关的调查，在科技行业有多大比例的人在不同程度上挣扎于这类事情？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: For the last two years, I've been doing a lot of writing, and most of my writing has really just been me opening up and sharing this personal side of what was going on behind the scenes. Along the way, I've been able to connect with, at this point, hundreds of folks in the tech industry who are dealing with their own forms of burnout or their own deep existential questions that are coming to the surface and they're trying to understand them. (00:13:48): So from some of the surveys I've put out from my own anecdotal experience and from some proper research that's been conducted by experts who focus on entrepreneur and high performer wellbeing, I'd say that it's a fair estimate to say that at least 50% to 60% of tech employees who have, just to give it a bit more nuance, who have been in the saddle, so to speak, for a minimum of five to seven years, they're experiencing some form of psychological and emotional distress. It may be minor enough such that they think it's just day-to-day anxiety, but it's often much more significant than people realize because, again, it creeps up on you slowly and then all of a sudden it hits you quickly.
turns.zh: 过去两年我一直在写很多东西，我的写作大多就是我在打开自己、分享这些幕后发生的个人一面。一路走来，我得以与——到现在为止——科技行业里数百位正在应对自己形式的倦怠或正在浮现的深层存在主义问题并试图理解它们的人建立了联系。(00:13:48)：所以根据我发出去的一些调查、我自己的轶事经验、以及一些由专注于创业者和高成就者幸福感的专家所做的正式研究，我觉得一个公平的估计是：至少 50% 到 60% 的科技员工——稍微给点更细致的限定——就是那些已经'在马鞍上'至少五到七年的——正在经历某种形式的心理和情感困扰。可能轻微到他们以为只是日常焦虑，但通常比人们意识到的要严重得多，因为同样，它慢慢爬上你，然后突然一下子击中你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to dive into what this looks like and ways you've found to be helpful to people. One last question before we get there. You walked away from a pretty senior incredible role, and in the post that you wrote, you shared the salary you gave up in that giving up. Can you just talk about what that last role was and then what you had to give up to change career paths and [inaudible 00:15:05]
turns.zh: 我们会深入探讨这看起来是什么样、以及你发现的对人们有帮助的方法。在进入之前最后一个问题。你离开了一个相当高级、令人难以置信的职位，在你写的那篇文章里，你分享了你放弃的薪水。你能谈谈最后一个职位是什么、然后你为了改变职业路径放弃了什么吗？（听不清）

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah. So one of the things that I did towards the tail end of my career as I became a consumer or founding partner of the consumer arm of an early stage venture capital firm, and most folks know that especially once a fund gets big enough, it can be a high paying job. Suddenly, I found myself in a position where I was making high six figures per year into early seven figures. When I look back on it in retrospect, I had put in so much effort to get to that point really going back to when I was 10 years old, having always been the straight A student and captain of whatever team I was on. (00:15:46): From the age of 10 to basically 35, I was switched on, constantly seeking to perform at the top of whatever my field was. So I gotten to that point first as an executive at a high growth startup, that was Wealthfront, and I became president and was next in line to be CEO before I had a health scare with my heart that led to me stepping away from the company because I knew I couldn't take on the CEO position. Then here I was six or seven months later, again, very subconsciously driven by the desire to succeed because underneath that was the sense that I wasn't lovable unless I was succeeding. (00:16:30): Here I was after a heart attack scare at the age of 35 sweeping that under the carpet like I'd swept so much stuff under the carpet and choosing to join on as a founding partner of a venture capital firm, which is not an easy job at all, and especially when you're starting a new firm up, it's, in a lot of ways, it's a company in and of its own. So it was another startup. It was my sixth startup in a row. (00:16:59): So three years into that though, even though I was working on my own mental health and my emotional wellbeing, I had convinced myself repeatedly for so many years that everything was okay and that I could continue to put my head down and run through these walls, these professional walls and keep going, but it got to a point to where that was no longer the case. (00:17:32): In fact, it was the culmination of conversations with my doctors and with the experts that I've been working with where I ended up actually spending 45 days in a mental health institute myself. It was something that was extremely difficult to do. It was something that certainly contributed or was really the tip of the sphere of me stepping away from my career of realizing that the only reason I was continuing to push forward despite how poorly I felt on the inside was because of stuff that had happened to me when I was much younger and because of the fallible nature of the human mind and how it wants to interpret experiences and ways that can become so self-critical and self damaging. (00:18:32): So that happened for me roughly three years ago. Needless to say, my life has changed quite a bit since then, and I'm happy to chat more about that, but that was a difficult decision to walk away from my career at the peak of it, but I guess the takeaway, and then I'll stop for a bit, is it's important for people to understand that there are formative experiences in our lives which put us in positions to where we form adaptations in order to survive, just like my attachment to achievement and how my self-worth was entirely tied up in that. (00:19:14): I needed that when I was younger because I was heartbroken, I lost a parent, and that adaptation that I formed saved my life when I was young, and it gave me a great childhood after that, and a great next couple of decades, but these adaptations, if you're unaware of them and if you're unaware of the subconscious drivers that are responsible for them, they run the risk that they go too far, and that these adaptations, which were initially beneficial to you and to your life, they reverse course in a sense, and they become detrimental to your present state and your future development. (00:20:04): So my stepping away from the career, stepping away from the high salary, and stepping away from everything I'd worked so hard to obtain was an action that I took in recognition of the fact that that early life adaptation had now gone awry and was responsible for my life heading in a negative direction and it was time to change.
turns.zh: 好的。我在职业生涯末期做的一件事是，我成为了一家早期风险投资公司消费部门的消费合伙人或创始合伙人。大多数人都知道，尤其是一只基金做到足够大之后，这可以是一份高薪工作。突然间我发现自己处于一个年收入高六位数到七位数早期的位置。回想起来，我付出了那么多努力才达到那一点，真的要追溯到我 10 岁的时候，一直是个全 A 学生、不管在哪个队都是队长。(00:15:46)：从 10 岁到基本上 35 岁，我都是开着的，不断地寻求在我所在的领域做到顶尖。所以我先是作为一家高增长创业公司 Wealthfront 的高管达到那一点，我做到了总裁，并且是下一任 CEO 的候选人，然后我 35 岁时心脏出了健康问题，导致我离开了公司，因为我知道我没法承担 CEO 的位置。然后六七个月后，我又——非常潜意识地被成功的欲望驱动着，因为那底下是'除非我在成功否则我不可爱'的感觉。(00:16:30)：于是我在 35 岁心脏病发作的惊魂之后，像扫掉很多东西一样把那件事扫到地毯下面，然后选择加入一家风险投资公司做创始合伙人——这绝不是一份轻松的工作，尤其当你在创办一家新公司时，在很多方面它本身就是一家公司。所以又是另一家创业公司，是我连续第六家创业公司。(00:16:59)：三年后，尽管我一直在处理自己的心理健康和情感幸福，我多年来一直反复说服自己一切都没事，我可以继续埋头冲破这些职业之墙、继续前进，但到了一个不再是这样的时候。(00:17:32)：事实上，是与我的医生和与我合作的专家们的对话的累积，让我最终自己在一家心理健康机构住了 45 天。这是一件极其困难的事。它确实是、或者说真的是我离开职业生涯的尖端——意识到我之所以继续向前推进、尽管我内心感觉那么糟糕，唯一的原因是发生在我小时候的事，以及人类心智的易错性、它如何以变得如此自我批评和自我破坏的方式来解读经历。(00:18:32)：所以那大概三年前发生。不消说，从那以后我的生活变了很多，我很乐意多聊聊那方面，但那是在巅峰时期离开职业生涯的一个艰难决定。但我想关键——然后我就停一下——是让人们理解，我们生命中有一些塑造性的经历，让我们处于形成适应方式以求生存的位置，就像我对成就的依附、以及我的自我价值如何完全被它绑住。(00:19:14)：我小时候需要它，因为我心碎了，我失去了一位父母。我形成的那个适应方式在我小时候救了我的命，它给了我之后很棒的童年和很棒的接下来二十年。但这些适应方式，如果你不知道它们、如果你不知道负责它们的潜意识驱动因素，它们就有走得太远的风险，这些最初对你和你的生活有益的适应方式，在某种意义上逆转方向，变得对你现在的状态和未来的发展有害。(00:20:04)：所以我离开职业生涯、离开高薪、离开我那么努力获得的一切，是我采取的一个行动，认识到那个早期生活的适应方式现在已经走偏了、正在让我的生活走向负面方向，是时候改变了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The gift of your experience going through all that is that now we can all benefit learning from that. You spend your time these days helping people get over a lot of these challenges that they have. Can you just talk about what it is you spend your time on specifically? Then let's unpack the process that you've come up with to help people through this.
turns.zh: 你经历这一切的礼物是现在我们都可以从中受益。你这些天花时间帮人们克服他们面临的很多挑战。你能具体讲讲你现在花时间做什么吗？然后我们来拆解你总结出来帮人度过这个的过程。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Now, when people ask me what I do, I say I do mental health advocacy, and I do it in a few ways. One is I sit on the board of a nonprofit called Heroic Hearts Project, and what we do is we raise money so that we can pay for military veterans with PTSD to get access to alternative therapies, namely psychedelic assisted psychotherapy. It was started by a handful of veterans. I was lucky enough to meet a few of them a couple of years ago. Given my own personal experience with PTSD stemming from my childhood experiences, I was bonded together with these men and women of the Armed Forces who had, in many cases, not only their own personal trauma, but also war trauma. So that's one organization that I'm thankful to be able to work with and help out. (00:21:48): I also write my newsletter and have created a new website that I'm toying with. In general, my writing and the content that I've put out is focused on the unhappy achievers, the other folks like myself who are out there, which there's quite a few of us. I write in order to express my personal experience because I think there's many others that can relate. turns.zh: 现在当人们问我做什么，我说我做心理健康倡导，我用几种方式做。一个是我是一家叫 Heroic Hearts Project 的非营利组织的董事会成员，我们做的事是筹款，以便让患有 PTSD 的退伍军人能获得替代疗法，即迷幻剂辅助的心理治疗。它由一群退伍军人创办。我有幸几年前认识了其中几位。鉴于我自己源自童年经历的 PTSD 个人经历，我跟这些武装力量的男女们联系在一起，他们很多时候不仅有自己的个人创伤，还有战争创伤。所以那是我很庆幸能参与和帮助的一个组织。(00:21:48)：我也写我的 newsletter，创建了一个我正在玩的新网站。总的来说，我的写作和输出的内容聚焦于'不开心的成就者'——其他像我一样的人，我们有相当多。我写作是为了表达我的个人经历，因为我觉得有很多其他人能产生共鸣。所以这些是我一直在做的事，外加一些对高成就者的辅导。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Throw out the website in case people want to check it out while we're talking.
turns.zh: 把网站说一下，以防大家在我们聊的时候想去看看。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: The website that I'm playing around with is called Clues.Life, clues as in questions, clues, not truth dot life or facts dot life. I called it Clues Dot Life for a reason because if there's one thing that I've learned in my own personal journey, it's that given the immense heterogeneity of the human population and how we're all born unique and then we're made further unique through our own individual life experiences, the thing that's clear to me is that if somebody is going through their own struggles, at the end of the day, they have to find the philosophies, the tools, and the methods that work for them. (00:23:08): You can read plenty of studies, you can read the books, you can listen to what others are doing, but at the end of the day, you got to personalize it to yourself. So that's why I called it Clues Dot Life because I'm building this library of mental health information that allows people to navigate all of this information in search of their own clues.
turns.zh: 我在玩的网站叫 Clues.Life，clues 是问题、线索的 clues——不是 truth.life 或 facts.life。我叫它 Clues.Life 是有原因的，因为如果在我的个人旅程中学到了一件事，那就是鉴于人类人口的巨大异质性、我们生来独特然后又通过各自的生活经历变得更加独特，对我来说清楚的是，如果有人正在经历自己的挣扎，归根结底他们必须找到适合自己的哲学、工具和方法。(00:23:08)：你可以读很多研究、读书、听别人在做什么，但归根结底，你得把它个性化到自己身上。所以我叫它 Clues.Life，因为我在建这个心理健康信息库，让人们可以在所有这些信息中导航、寻找自己的线索。
