turns.en: Awesome, and we'll link to that in the show notes, but it's an easy URL to remember. Something you spent a lot of your time on as you've talked about is helping people through deep personal transformation. That's the way you describe it. What is involved in that process of someone going through a deep personal transformation?
turns.zh: 太好了，我们会在 show notes 里放链接，不过这个 URL 很好记。你花很多时间做的、如你所说的事，是帮助人们进行深度个人转化。你是这么描述的。一个人进行深度个人转化的过程涉及什么？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: I love this question. So most of the conversations I have are with folks who are going through significant change. Now, what's involved in that? It can happen on a spectrum where everyone's process is unique. We all change and unfold in identical ways. Some can go through subtle shifts. I've heard this referred to as a micro transition, where, for example, they may be working at a tech industry or at a tech company, but this specific company they're working at, they have no real values connection to it. So part of their suffering is the fact that they feel that the work that they're doing doesn't really matter or they don't feel a connection to it. So switching to work at a different company that's aligned with something that's consistent with their values, that may be enough for somebody to go through a small transition and then find themselves in a happier place. (00:24:52): The transitions that I talk about are the big fundamental ones like the transition that I've been going through myself. Now, what's involved in that? I think that there are four parts, just to give it a simple general framework. Step one is it begins with suffering. These large transitions in life rarely take place in the absence of suffering. So step number one is suffer. Usually, the deeper somebody suffers, the more significant the transition that may follow. There's a reason why in the 12 steps community like Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, you name it, there's a reason that rock bottom is in the vernacular because rock bottom tends to proceed somebody getting sober. So step one is suffering. (00:25:53): Step two is seeking the truth behind why we suffer. Once the suffering gets so bad in somebody through some spiritual intervention, a legal intervention, the intervention of friends and family, whatever it may be, they decide to change, and in order to change, you have to understand the truth as to who you are and why you are the way you are and why you're suffering. The answer lies in understanding the truth, and that is usually a long process. Digging through the subconscious mind, digging through your history and your past, digging through your relationships, that takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of time to remove the mental blocks that we might've spent decades developing such that we don't even see these patterns that we play out regularly. (00:26:51): So first, you begin with suffering, and then second, you seek the truth for your suffering. What I have found, and that leads to step three in the process, is that once you discover the truth of your suffering, the real root cause of it and where it came from, that's when you move to step three, which is you begin to experience and to practice self-compassion and self-love because inevitably, what you discover through this process of seeking the truth is that your suffering isn't necessarily your fault. Maybe you're suffering because of things that you experienced or had to go through of which you had no control over. (00:27:44): Nonetheless, it's common for the mind, especially the mind of a child, to interpret those less than nurturing experiences as, "This happened because of me." So what sits at the core of their suffering is not only a low sense of self, but a shame, a shame regarding who they are and who they believe themselves to be. (00:28:08): When you dig deep enough into your own self-understanding, eventually you'll discover that that's not true, that it isn't your fault, that these things swept you up like a wave, and you were just along for a ride of which you had no choice. When you understand that and you start to feel a sense of forgiveness and to begin to love yourself for the first time, you make this switch where then you're willing to live in a way that is more consistent with self-love and self-compassion. (00:28:45): So me, for example, stepping away from my career, at the end of the day, I wasn't running from something, I was running back towards myself. That was an act of kindness towards myself. Going into a 45-day hospitalization, that was an act of love. So what ends up happening is the truth fuels that process of self-love, and when you begin to live in a way that is consistent with valuing yourself and understanding that it's not your fault, then that's when you move to step four, which is compassion towards others because by understanding yourself and realizing the true nature of why you are the way you are and forgiving yourself because you understand it's not your fault, guess what? You see the same thing in everybody else. (00:29:46): This is what is meant when folks sometimes say we're all adults or we're all children walking around in adult bodies, right? We're just acting out the things that were done to us in the past because when I think of the human mind, there are many ways that you can describe what the brain is, but one way that I describe it certainly is that it's autobiographical. It tries to predict what's going to happen next based on what happened in the past. It's a prediction engine. That's what it does, and that's why I say it's autobiographical because the way that you present yourself to the world as an adult is a reflection of what happened to you in the past, the messages you were told, the ways you were conditioned by society, maybe the traumas you experienced. (00:30:36): So that's the process as I see it of deep, deep, deep transformation. It's that four-step process of the suffering, the seeking of truth, the living in a way that is compassionate towards oneself, and then living in a way that is compassionate towards others. When you do that, you change. Think of that as the horizontal foundation to which the rest of your external life is built. The place you choose to live, the partner you choose to have, the friends you have, the career you have, all of these things are erections on top of a foundation of identity, and that identity is what is completely rewired when somebody goes through that four-step process, and as a result, everything that's built on top of that identity, it doesn't necessarily have to change, but it might.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。我进行的大多数对话都是跟正在经历重大变化的人。那涉及什么呢？它可以发生在一个光谱上，每个人的过程都是独特的。我们都以独特的方式变化和展开。有些人会经历微妙的转变，我听说过这被称为'微转化'——比如，他们可能在科技行业或科技公司工作，但这家具体的公司他们没有真正的价值观连接。所以他们的一部分痛苦是他们觉得做的工作没什么意义、或者他们感觉不到与它的连接。所以换到一家与他们价值观一致的公司工作，可能就足够让一个人经历一次小的转变，然后到达一个更快乐的地方。(00:24:52)：我谈的转变是那些大的根本性的，比如我一直在经历的那种。那涉及什么呢？我觉得有四个部分，给它一个简单的通用框架。第一步是它从痛苦开始。这些人生的大转变很少在缺乏痛苦的情况下发生。所以第一步是痛苦。通常一个人痛苦得越深，随之而来的转变可能越重大。在 12 步社区比如匿名戒酒会、匿名戒毒会里有原因把'rock bottom'作为常用词——因为 rock bottom 往往发生在一个人戒酒之前。所以第一步是痛苦。(00:25:53)：第二步是寻找我们为什么痛苦的真相。一旦痛苦变得太严重，通过某种精神介入、法律介入、亲友介入，无论是什么，他们决定改变。要改变，你必须理解关于你是谁、你为什么是这样、你为什么痛苦的真相。答案在于理解真相，而那通常是一个漫长的过程。挖掘潜意识、挖掘你的历史和过去、挖掘你的人际关系——那需要很多时间。需要很多时间来移除我们可能花了几十年发展出来的心智障碍，以至于我们甚至看不到自己经常上演的这些模式。(00:26:51)：所以首先你从痛苦开始，然后第二你寻找痛苦的真相。我发现——这引到第三步——一旦你发现了痛苦的真相、真正的根本原因以及它从哪里来，你就进入第三步：你开始体验和实践自我同情和自爱。因为不可避免地，你通过这个寻找真相的过程发现的，是你的痛苦不一定是你的错。也许你痛苦是因为你经历的、不得不经历的你无法控制的事情。(00:27:44)：尽管如此，心智——尤其是孩子的心智——很常见地把那些不够滋养的经历解读为'这发生是因为我'。所以他们痛苦的核心不仅是低自我价值感，还有一种羞耻——关于他们是谁、他们相信自己是谁的羞耻。(00:28:08)：当你足够深地挖掘自己的自我理解，最终你会发现那不是真的，那不是你的错，那些事情像海浪一样把你卷走，你只是搭了一程你没法选择的 ride。当你理解了那个、开始感觉到一种原谅、第一次开始爱自己的时候，你就做了一个转变，然后你愿意以更符合自爱和自我同情的方式生活。(00:28:45)：比如我，离开我的职业生涯，归根结底我不是在逃离什么，我是在跑回我自己。那是对自己的一种善意。住进 45 天的医院，那是一种爱的行为。所以发生的是真相为那个自爱的过程提供燃料，当你开始以符合重视自己、理解那不是你的错的方式生活时，你就进入第四步：对他人的同情。因为通过理解自己、意识到你为什么是这样的真相、因为理解那不是你的错而原谅自己——你猜怎么着？你在其他人身上看到同样的东西。(00:29:46)：这就是有时候人们说'我们都只是成人、或者我们都只是在成人身体里走动的孩子'的意思，对吧？我们只是在演出过去对我们做过的事情。因为当我想到人类心智——有很多方式可以描述大脑是什么——但我描述它的一种方式肯定是它是自传式的。它试图基于过去发生的事预测接下来会发生什么。它是一个预测引擎。这就是它做的，这就是我说它自传式的原因，因为作为成人你呈现给世界的方式，是你过去发生的事情的反映——别人告诉你的信息、社会 conditioning 你的方式、也许你经历的创伤。(00:30:36)：所以这就是我所看到的深度、深度、深度转化的过程。就是那四步——痛苦、寻找真相、以对自己同情的方式生活、然后以对他人同情的方式生活。当你那样做，你就改变了。把它想成是你其他外在生活建在上面的水平地基。你选择住的地方、你选择的伴侣、你的朋友、你的职业，所有这些都是身份认同地基上面的建筑，而那个身份认同就是当一个人经历那四步过程时被完全重新布线的东西，结果是建立在那身份认同之上的一切——不一定需要改变，但可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That feels like a reason somebody wouldn't want to go down this journey of, "I don't want to change everything about myself."
turns.zh: 这听起来像是人们不想走这条路的一个理由——'我不想改变关于自己的一切'。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yes, and this is the power of the human mind at work or what someone referred to as the ego. As soon as the ego senses that something wants to challenge it and to undermine its authority, it finds a way to push it away. It finds a way to ignore it because it is a very difficult process. I now understand what some philosophers described as death before dying. In this process of change that I've been going through, it's been the death of the old me, the death of Andy whose identity was entirely attached to succeeding, and that old Andy doesn't want to let go. It's been around for a few decades. It believes that it's there to protect me. (00:32:46): This is a survival mechanism that's somewhat gone awry within the context of modern life. So it doesn't want to let go, but that's what I've been doing. That's the process I've been going through is slowly but surely finding a way to take my fingers off the steering wheel and to let that old sense of self die, and then in doing so create the room for what's next, whatever that may be. I'm three years into the process of discovering what that will be. So we'll see.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是人类心智的力量——或某些人所说的自我——在起作用。一旦自我感觉到有东西想挑战它、削弱它的权威，它就找到办法推开它。它找到办法忽略它，因为这是一个非常困难的过程。我现在理解一些哲学家所描述的'死亡先于死亡'。在我一直在经历的这个改变过程中，它是旧的我、那个身份完全依附于成功的 Andy 的死亡，而那个旧 Andy 不想放手。它已经存在了几十年。它相信它在那里是为了保护我。(00:32:46)：这是一种在现代生活的背景下有点失控的生存机制。所以它不想放手，但那就是我一直在做的。我一直在经历的过程就是慢慢地、但确定地找到一种方式把我的手指从方向盘上拿开，让那个旧的自我感死去，然后这样做就为什么是下一个腾出空间，无论那是什么。我已经进入这个过程三年了，正在发现那会是什么。我们走着看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thinking through these four steps, suffering sounds like people will just do that naturally, potentially, and I feel like it gets hard at the understanding the source of that suffering. I guess, one, is that true or do people try to resist that suffering and are just like, "Nah, it's okay, it's okay," and they white knuckle it?
turns.zh: 想想这四个步骤，痛苦听起来人们会自然地经历，潜在地，我觉得难就难在理解那个痛苦的根源。我猜，第一，这是真的吗？还是人们试图抗拒那个痛苦、就是'不，没事，没事'，然后硬扛？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: I think you're pretty spot on with it. This dips into a lot of the ancient Eastern spiritual traditions of just this recognition that life involves suffering. One way or another, there's going to be suffering. I think of it as there's two types of suffering. There's the necessary suffering like we're going to get old and our bodies are going to hurt and we're going to have physical ailments and toothaches and shit's just going to happen and we're going to lose the people we love, all of us, and the 80 to a hundred billion homo sapiens that live before us gone through the same thing. (00:34:29): So there is necessary suffering in life or the mandatory suffering, and then there's the unnecessary suffering, which is the suffering that is almost entirely, and I think the argument could be made that it's entirely made up in our minds. This is the superpowers of the human mind gone awry again in the modern context. So there's going to be a lot of suffering one way or another. I think if there's a goal or objective, it's to minimize the unnecessary suffering, but the seeking of the truth part is very difficult. It takes years. (00:35:10): There's a reason that, again, in some of these spiritual traditions, let's take Buddhism for example, there's a reason that there's so much structure and discipline and there's a daily method that they adhere to because it turns out it takes daily practice. In the same way that if you want to get extremely fit and climb Mount Everest, that's not something you do by just getting off the couch, right? It takes a dedication to it. I think that the seeking of truth takes that dedication, and that's, again, why I believe that the first step is almost always suffering because to undergo that process of personal transformation, which can be very difficult, and it can feel like you're in a life raft and you've just pushed away from the shore completely untethered, uncertain of where you're floating. In order to work up the courage to get to that point, things typically have to get pretty bad. (00:36:09): You say, "I can't fucking do this anymore. I'm not going to live like this. Something's got to change." So much of that seeking of the truth is actually at first driven by intense fear, fear of going back to how bad things were and feeling that bad again. Eventually, the process changes tone when you move past the fear stage and you understand yourself enough and then you start to look forward optimistically towards the future, where instead of just being driven by fear, you're also pulled forward by a vision for the future that inspires you. So that eventually comes, but to begin with, yes, this process of discovering the truth is very, very, very, very difficult. It requires a personal commitment. It's not something anyone else can do for you.
turns.zh: 我觉得你说得很准。这涉及到很多古老的东方精神传统——就是这种认识：人生包含痛苦。一种或另一种方式，会有痛苦。我把它想成有两种痛苦。一种是必要的痛苦，比如我们会老、身体会疼、会有身体疾病和牙痛之类的事会发生、我们会失去我们爱的人——我们所有人，以及在我们之前活过的 800 亿到 1000 亿智人都经历过同样的事。(00:34:29)：所以人生中有必要的痛苦，或者说强制的痛苦，然后有不必要的痛苦——那种几乎完全是、我觉得可以论证完全是我们的心智编造出来的痛苦。这是人类心智的超能力在现代语境下再次失控。所以无论如何会有很多痛苦。我觉得如果有一个目标或目的，那就是最小化不必要的痛苦。但寻找真相的部分非常困难，需要好几年。(00:35:10)：有原因——再说一次——在这些精神传统里，比如佛教，有那么多的结构和纪律、他们 adhering to 的日常方法，因为事实证明它需要日常练习。就像你想变得极其健壮去爬珠穆朗玛峰，那不是你从沙发上起来就能做到的，对吧？它需要投入。我觉得寻找真相需要那种投入，这也就是为什么我相信第一步几乎总是痛苦，因为要经历那个个人转化的过程——它非常困难，它可以感觉像你在一只救生筏上，刚刚离开岸边，完全 untethered，不确定你飘向哪里。要鼓起勇气到达那一点，事情通常得变得相当糟糕。(00:36:09)：你说'我他妈的再也受不了了，我不要再这样活了，有些事必须改变'。寻找真相的那么多其实在最初是由强烈的恐惧驱动的——害怕回到事情有多糟、再次感觉那么糟。最终，当你越过恐惧阶段、对自己足够理解，这个过程会改变基调，你开始乐观地展望未来，那时你不只是被恐惧驱动，你也被一个启发你的未来愿景所牵引。那个最终会来，但开始的时候是的，这个发现真相的过程非常非常非常非常困难。它需要个人承诺。这不是别人能替你做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that context in mind that it's very difficult, I imagine many people listening are like, "Yes, I have a lot of suffering that I'm going through. Life is hard, work is hard, work is too crazy," especially product managers and founders that listen to this podcast.
turns.zh: 知道这个背景——它非常困难——我猜很多听众会想'是的，我正在经历很多痛苦，生活很难，工作很难，工作太疯狂'，尤其是听这个播客的产品经理和创始人。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: I know. To all the VPs of Product out there, I'm so sorry. I've been in your shoes.
turns.zh: 我知道。对所有产品 VP 们，我非常抱歉，我穿过你们的鞋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So with that, say someone wanted to go down this path and understand the truth of what is the source of this suffering that you even described as unnecessary and made up, what would the first couple steps be of knowing that it's going to take years potentially of how to actually try to understand this?
turns.zh: 那么，假设有人想走这条路、想理解你描述为不必要的、编造的痛苦根源是什么，知道这可能会花好几年，最初几步是什么？怎么实际尝试理解这个？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Commonly in the West, the first step that makes a lot of sense is you turn to somebody who's trained in helping you figure out what those truths are, which is a therapist or a psychologist or a psychiatrist or a counselor. Sometimes people turn to religious or spiritual leaders because they can be quite gifted in this as well. That's the most common step. (00:38:02): That's the first step that I turn to when I was just completely stricken by panic and terrified that I might harm myself. I said, "I got to figure out what the hell's going on because I can't live feeling like this," and all I knew to do was reach out to a therapist, and that is a wonderful first start because if anything, they're not going to have all the answers, but they can act like a router, where as they're helping you understand yourself and they're really understanding you, they're thinking about, "Okay. Who might this person also benefit from speaking with? Let's route them to this person that specializes in body-based work, somatic work. Let's send this person to somebody that specializes in nervous system management through breath work or other things." So seeking a therapist is a pretty good first step.
turns.zh: 在西方，通常最有意义的第一步是找一个受过训练、帮你弄清楚那些真相是什么的人——也就是治疗师、心理学家、精神科医生或咨询师。有时候人们转向宗教或精神领袖，因为他们在这方面也可以很有天赋。这是最常见的一步。(00:38:02)：这就是我最初走的一步，那时我完全被恐慌击中、害怕我可能伤害自己。我说：'我得搞清楚到底他妈的怎么了，因为我没法再这样活了'，我唯一知道做的就是找治疗师。那是一个非常棒的第一步，因为即使他们不会有所有答案，他们可以像一个路由器——当他们帮你理解自己、理解你的时候，他们在想：'好吧，这个人还能从跟谁谈话中受益？让我们把他路由到这个专门做身体工作、体感工作的人。让我们把这个人送给一个通过呼吸工作或其他方式做神经系统管理的人。'所以找治疗师是一个相当好的第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any advice on how to figure out who the right therapist or wrong therapist is for you? I know you've actually shared somewhere on LinkedIn once that there's also a lot of disagreement within the mental health community of what is the right approach and what's the right solution.
turns.zh: 关于怎么判断谁是合适的治疗师、谁是不合适的治疗师，你有什么建议吗？我知道你曾经在 LinkedIn 上分享过，心理健康社区内部也有很多分歧，关于什么是正确的方法、什么是正确的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: It's like speed dating at first because I would argue that the most important factor is that you feel safe. Animals can teach us so much about what it means to heal ourselves. Imagine going to the pound and you go in there and there's a bunch of dogs that have been picked up off the street or that have been abandoned, and the vast majority of them, they're a nervous wreck, right? Their tail is down in between their legs. They're hunched over and they might be shaking. Their nervous system is completely overwhelmed. That is not the time to teach a dog tricks. When the dog still can't come out the corner of the kennel is not the time to teach it how to sit. Once that dog can make it into the arms of an owner that it feels safe with and loved by, that's when you see the dog transform and change, and that's when you can teach it a lot because it's open and receptive to it. (00:40:21): So that's number one in my advice is speed date if you've got the opportunity to and try out a few therapists and just go based on intuition, what just feels right to you, and you're going to want to fall into that feeling of comfort. Now, a quick asterisk on that. Of course if you're in real distress, if you're in a bad place, just see whatever professional you can as soon as possible. That's what I did. I was fortunate to where the first one that I saw was also fantastic. I ended up seeing many other specialists over the years, but that first one, she was wonderful. (00:41:05): So it's essential that you feel comfortable with them. I would also say, this one's a little controversial, but you're going to want a therapist that is at least as intelligent, if not more intelligent than you because I think part of that openness to learning from them and to feeling somewhat comfortable but also feeling inspired and looking forward to it as if sometimes they say things that make you say, "Oh, shit. Wow. Wow, I never thought of that. That was smart," or, "That was a wonderful insight." I don't think if you respect their intellectual abilities, then it's going to be difficult for them to help you. They may not be able to communicate on the same wavelength. So you really want to look for that intuitive feeling of something that is safe and comfortable. Ideally, if you can find somebody with some intellectual horsepower that matches your own, honestly, I think the rest after that is just implementation details.
turns.zh: 一开始就像速配一样，因为我会说最重要的因素是你感到安全。动物可以教我们很多关于疗愈自己意味着什么。想象你去收容所，里面有一堆被从街上捡回来的或被遗弃的狗，它们中绝大多数是紧张兮兮的，对吧？尾巴夹在腿中间，蜷缩着，可能在发抖。它们的神经系统完全过载。那不是教狗把戏的时候。当狗还没法走出 kennel 的角落时，不是教它坐下的时候。一旦那只狗能进入它觉得安全、被爱的主人的怀抱，你就会看到狗转变和改变，那时你可以教它很多，因为它开放和接受。(00:40:21)：所以这是我的第一条建议：如果有机会的话，速配，试几个治疗师，就凭直觉——什么感觉对。你会想陷入那种舒适感。关于这个一个快速的注脚：当然如果你真的处于困境、在一个糟糕的地方，就看你能看到的任何专业人士、尽快。这就是我做的。我很幸运，我看到的第一个就很棒。这些年来我看过很多其他专家，但第一个，她非常棒。(00:41:05)：所以跟他们在一起感到舒适是关键。我还想说——这条有点争议——你会想要一个至少跟你一样聪明、如果不比你更聪明的治疗师，因为我觉得那种向他们学习的开放性、感到某种程度的舒适但同时也感到受启发、期待去见他们——就好像有时候他们说一些话让你说：'哦，靠，哇，我从没那样想过，那真聪明'或者'那是个很棒的洞察'。我觉得如果你尊重他们的智识能力，那会很难帮到你。他们可能没法在同一个波长上沟通。所以你真的要寻找那种直觉的、安全舒适的感觉。理想情况下，如果你能找到一个智识马力跟你匹配的人，老实说，剩下的就只是实施细节了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone maybe isn't ready for a therapist and that's something about that just holds them back, is there another route that you would recommend people take or is it just go straight to a therapist?
turns.zh: 如果有人可能还没准备好找治疗师，有什么东西让他们犹豫，你会推荐人们走另一条路吗？还是就直接去找治疗师？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Absolutely. Absolutely. If you're not in a state of distress, but you feel like there's something to be figured out, there's an ancient technology known as pen and paper. At the end of the day, the seeking of the truth involves the seeking of a deep sense of self-understanding, and if you can get into the daily practice of being able to sit down with pen and paper and write to yourself, to ask yourself questions, to really sit there and evaluate the thoughts that are running through your head, it is possible for somebody to, and I'll use the term, I won't get into it, but to reach some state of bliss or enlightenment or some real spiritual awakening, it is possible for somebody to do that entirely on their own with just pen and paper and a quiet room. (00:43:20): I know people that have arrived at a deep place of self-love and self-understanding through those methods, and I know a lot of others, including myself, where the writing to others was really the writing to myself 15 years ago as a way for me to continue to understand myself more deeply. So I think pen and paper is deeply, deeply overlooked and underrated in this process.
turns.zh: 绝对，绝对。如果你不是处于困境状态，但你觉得有什么需要弄清楚，有一种古老的技术叫纸和笔。归根结底，寻找真相涉及寻求一种深度的自我理解，如果你能进入每天坐下来用纸笔给自己写、问自己问题、真的坐在那里评估脑子里跑过的想法的日常练习，一个人是有可能——我不会展开——达到某种 bliss 或启蒙或某种真正的精神觉醒的状态的，一个人完全靠自己、只用纸和笔和一个安静的房间是有可能做到的。(00:43:20)：我认识一些人通过那些方法达到了一个深度的自爱和自我理解的地方，我也认识很多其他人——包括我自己——其中写给别人的东西其实真的就是我 15 年前写给自己、作为继续更深入理解自己的一种方式。所以我觉得纸和笔在这个过程中被深深深深低估了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say you get a pen and paper, is there some guide or framework or something you'd point people to you to think through what to think about and how to approach this?
turns.zh: 假设你拿了纸笔，有什么指南或框架或什么你会指向人们去思考要思考什么、怎么接近这个的吗？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah. There are different ways of doing it. Some advocate for a completely unstructured approach because what you want is you don't want to turn it into assignment. You want to feel your way into it. If something is bubbling up in your mind, just spit it out. Don't analyze why it's coming up, just allow it to flow. That method certainly works. Sit down with no agenda. On some days you'll write one sentence and that's enough, and on other days you'll write 10 pages and that's also enough. There's some magic to allowing the human mind to just work and to not interrupt it through some analytical process. (00:44:40): On the flip side, if you want a little bit more structure, one thing you can do is I'd like to start with if the goal is to understand oneself, then one of the quickest ways of doing that is to quickly write down a list of simple bullet points of the most recent situations you can think of where you became most acutely reactionary and emotional. You could have been having a political conversation with somebody and they said something that really just you felt like you just wanted to reach out and strangle them. You could have felt deeply insecure in a social setting. (00:45:24): Just run through those scenarios where something disrupted what might've been your current state of presence and calmness. When you identify those situations where there was some strong reaction, that is very revealing because that wasn't a conscious thought process that led to the reaction. That was a knee-jerk reaction. That was a reflex. If there's a reflex, then there's something that's underlying the reflex, and the question to then ask is, "Why did that happen?" (00:45:58): Then from there, it's an unstructured process. Keep asking, keep digging, keep asking, "Okay. If this happened, why did that happen? Well ..." and then write a little bit, "Well, is that really the reason why? Was there something else?" Just keep working at it until you hit the truth, and you'll know what the truth is because it always feels either deeply uncomfortable or it feels like an epiphany.
turns.zh: 有的，有不同的方式做。有些人主张完全无结构的方式，因为你想要的是——你不想把它变成作业。你想感觉着进入它。如果有什么在你脑子里冒泡，就吐出来。不要分析它为什么冒出来，就让它流。那种方法确实有效。坐下来没有议程。有些天你会写一句话就够了，有些天你会写 10 页也够了。允许人类心智就那样工作、不通过某种分析过程打断它，其中有 magic。(00:44:40)：反过来，如果你想要多一点结构，你可以做的一件事是——我喜欢从如果目标是理解自己开始，那么最快的方式之一就是快速写下你能想到的最近的几个你变得最急性地反应性和情绪化的情况的简单要点。可能你在跟人进行政治对话，他们说了什么真的让你觉得你只想伸手掐死他们。可能你在某个社交场合感到深深的不安全。(00:45:24)：就过一遍那些有什么打破了你可能有的当下临在和平静状态的场景。当你识别出那些有强烈反应的情况，那非常揭示，因为那不是一个有意识的思考过程导致反应，那是一个 knee-jerk 反应，那是一个反射。如果有反射，那就有某种东西在反射之下，然后要问的问题是：'为什么那会发生？'(00:45:58)：然后从那里开始是一个无结构的过程。继续问，继续挖，继续问：'好，如果这个发生了，为什么那个会发生？嗯……'然后写一点：'嗯，那真的是原因吗？还有别的吗？'就继续 work at it 直到你撞到真相，你会知道什么是真相，因为它总是要么感觉深深不舒服，要么感觉像一个 epiphany。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. For you that was recognizing that it was about your mom.
turns.zh: 哇。对你来说那就是认识到这跟妈妈有关。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: There were many parts of it. At its core, at first it began with a simple truth, which was I went into the therapist, I was describing what I was feeling, I was describing the uncontrollable thoughts and mental imagery that I was experiencing, and my sleep disruption, and my pounding heart, and everything else, and she said, "Yup, you're having panic attacks," and just knowing like, "Oh, there's a thing and it's called a panic attack," starting at that basic truth was enough in the moment to just take a little bit of the edge off. (00:47:18): So this journey along the way is there are dozens of truths and then hundreds of truths, and then every now and then it's punctuated by the big, "Oh, holy shit. I never saw that coming," kind of truth. It's just what the experience is. I had many, many truths about myself that I discovered before I hit some of the fundamental ones that were at the core of my subconscious.
turns.zh: 有很多部分。在核心，最初开始于一个简单的真相——我进治疗师那里，我在描述我感觉到的，我在描述我正在经历的无法控制的想法和心理画面，我的睡眠紊乱，我跳动的心脏，以及其他一切，她说：'嗯，你在有恐慌发作'，就知道'哦，有一个东西叫恐慌发作'，从那个基本的真相开始，在那个时刻就足以让 edge 减一点。(00:47:18)：所以这条路上有几十个真相，然后几百个真相，然后偶尔被一个大的'哦，靠，我从没料到那个'的真相打断。这就是这个体验。在我达到一些处于我潜意识核心的根本性真相之前，我发现了关于自己的很多很多真相。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Following in that thread, what are signs that you're in need of this transformation versus, "Work is just stressful. Things are hard. I have some challenging meetings," which a lot of people go through on and off? I've had a lot of those. What are signs maybe you're boarding out or something that requires, "Wow, I really need to dig a lot deeper"?
turns.zh: 顺着这条线，什么迹象表明你需要这种转化，对比'工作就是有压力、事情就是难、我有一些挑战性的会议'——很多人会经历这些？我有过很多这种。什么迹象也许你在倦怠或者有什么需要'哇，我真的需要深挖很多'？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: There are day-to-day stresses that are normal and we just have to put up with, but then there's the other stuff that's the flashing red alarm. For me, and a lot of the research and literature supports this too, is, again, you can go back to animals. It's like when their fundamental functions, when their core behaviors of diet, exercise, playfulness, socialization, sleep, when those things get disrupted, it's a sign that there is something going on here that you need to take a look at. (00:48:49): So the same is true with people. If your sleep always sucks, if your relationships are constantly strained or frequently strained, if your physical health is failing, there's so many ways that that can be measured so there's really no excuse for that to say, "Oh, I just didn't know," I'd say it's to look at those things. When those are suffering or when they're really out of whack, it's undeniable that there is something that is detrimental to your wellbeing that's going on right now, and your body is telling you, "Stop. Something needs to change." So that is number one to look at. Look at the fundamentals. (00:49:43): Reflecting on my own situation, I almost had a heart attack at 35, and I got the classic talk from a Stanford cardiologist saying, "You're just going to be another 40-something-year-old CEO with a broken heart." The years of really poor sleep, the number of teeth that I had broken that I had to have fixed multiple times because for years my grinding was so bad that I had to, now two times over, had to completely redo all the teeth, all my molars, and then most of the front teeth as well, and I just continued to move forward even though my body was, again, throwing out all the signals. (00:50:31): For anyone who's listening to this, especially for the folks who haven't, go get the book, The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk. He's a expert clinician who's worked with trauma patients for decades, and the entire book is basically one big message saying, "Hey, when mental health presents itself, look to the body because it's the body that is keeping the score." It's the body that's the scoreboard, and it's the body that is actually holding on to all of this shit you've been carrying for years, and eventually, the body breaks in the form of chronic disease and illness and so on and so forth.
turns.zh: 有日常的压力是正常的，我们只能忍受；但还有另一种东西是闪烁的红色警报。对我来说——很多研究和文献也支持——同样，你可以回到动物身上——当它们的基本功能、核心行为——饮食、运动、玩耍、社交、睡眠——这些被打乱的时候，那就是一个信号，说明这里有什么事你需要看一看。(00:48:49)：人也是一样。如果你的睡眠总是很糟，如果你的人际关系经常或频繁地紧张，如果你的身体健康在恶化——有很多方式可以衡量，所以真的没有借口说'哦，我只是不知道'。我会说就看那些东西。当那些在受苦、真的失衡的时候，不可否认，有某种正在损害你幸福感的事情正在发生，你的身体在告诉你：'停下来，有些事需要改变。'这是第一要看的东西。看那些基本的东西。(00:49:43)：反思我自己的情况，我 35 岁时差点心脏病发作，斯坦福的心脏科医生给了我那个经典的谈话：'你只会是另一个 40 多岁心脏坏掉的 CEO。'那些年糟糕的睡眠，我断裂的、不得不修好多次的牙齿——因为好几年我磨牙那么严重，我不得不两次完全重做所有的牙齿、所有的臼齿，然后还有大部分前面的牙齿——我就是继续前进，即使我的身体在——再说一次——发出所有信号。(00:50:31)：对每个听众，尤其是那些还没读过的人，去读 Bessel van der Kolk 的《The Body Keeps the Score》。他是一位与创伤患者工作了几十年的专家临床医生，整本书基本上就是一个大信息：'嘿，当心理健康呈现自己的时候，看身体，因为是身体在记分。'身体是记分板，是身体实际上在 hold 住你这么多年来扛着的所有这些破事，最终，身体以慢性疾病和疾病等形式崩溃。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by Miro, an online collaborative whiteboard that's designed specifically for teams like yours. The best way to see what Miro is all about and how it can help your team collaborate better is not to listen to me talk about it, but to go check it out for yourself. Go to miro.com/lenny. With the help of the Miro team, I created a super cool Miro board with two of my own favorite templates, my one pager template and my managing up template that you can plug and play and start using immediately with your team. I've also embedded a handful of my favorite templates that other people have published in the Miroverse. When you get to the board, you can also leave suggestions for the podcast, answer a question that I have for you, and generally just play around to get a sense of how it all works. (00:51:56): Miro is a killer tool for brainstorming with your team, laying out your strategy, sharing user research findings, capturing ideas, giving feedback on wireframes, and generally just collaborating with your colleagues. I actually used Miro to collaborate with the Miro team on creating my own board, and it was super fun and super easy. Go check it out at miro.com/lenny. That's M-I-R-O dot com slash Lenny. (00:52:22): We've talked about the suffering step, then the understanding the truth of what is going on. Say someone sits down in a room, writes out what's going on, has this epiphany of, "Oh, wow, it's really this moment in my childhood that really led me to need to achieve and do all these things." The next step is self-compassion and recognizing that it's not your fault. That sounds very easy on the surface like, "Okay. I understand this is not my fault." I know it's not that easy. How do you go about actually deeply doing that steps?
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Miro 赞助，一个专门为像你这样的团队设计的在线协作白板。了解 Miro 是什么、它如何帮你的团队更好协作的最好方式不是听我讲，而是自己去看看。去 miro.com/lenny。在 Miro 团队的帮助下，我用我自己的两个最爱模板——我的 one-pager 模板和我的向上管理模板——创建了一个超酷的 Miro 看板，你可以即插即用立即跟团队开始用。我还嵌入了一些其他人在 Miroverse 上发布的我最爱的模板。当你到那个看板上，你还可以给播客留建议、回答我给你的一个问题，总体上就玩一下感受它是怎么运作的。(00:51:56)：Miro 是一个跟你的团队头脑风暴、布置战略、分享用户研究发现、捕捉想法、给 wireframe 反馈、总体上跟同事协作的杀手级工具。我其实就用 Miro 跟 Miro 团队协作创建了我自己的看板，超级好玩、超级简单。去 miro.com/lenny 看看。那就是 M-I-R-O.com/lenny。(00:52:22)：我们聊了痛苦这一步，然后是理解正在发生什么的真相。假设一个人坐在房间里，写下正在发生什么，有了一个 epiphany：'哦，哇，真的是我童年的这个时刻真的让我需要去成就、做所有这些事。'下一步是自我同情、认识到那不是你的错。表面上听起来很容易——'好，我理解这不是我的错'。我知道没那么容易。你实际怎么深入地做到那一步？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: It's likely this deeply internalized self-belief. You can think of that as one of the deepest grooves in the neural pathways in your mind. Now, that was the case for me, so deep that you don't even realize that it's there, it's omnipresent. It's going to take time to rewire that because what you're effectively trying to do is take an internal narrative and edit and rewrite that thing, and this internal narrative is probably at a foothold in you for years or decades. So it's reasonable to believe or to understand that, "Okay. If I have not had a high opinion of myself for 30 years, that's not going to change overnight." (00:53:50): For some people, it miraculously does. That's not the norm. For most others, including myself, it starts with that truth stage because with truth is the awareness, "Okay. I understand that I have a low sense of self-worth, and I understand that it plays out in all these ways, and I have the awareness of it that now when I'm doing something that is a conditioned behavior or a conditioned response born out of that deep self-belief or that negative core belief, then when I spot it, there's an opportunity for me to intervene," and it starts in the simple ways. (00:54:31): For example, I had a boss once where he would come over and he would give me praise all the time. He was wonderful human being, and I think I was doing a good job. One day, he swung by, he said, "Hey, amazing job," and my response was, "Oh, yeah, I did my best," and then he looked at me and he said, "Hey, say thank you or you're welcome. That's it. When somebody gives you a compliment, just say thanks, accept it." So it's become a pattern of mine now that if somebody gives me a compliment, I look them in the eyes and I say, "Thank you," and I really try and embrace that little moment because it's in all of those ways where you identify these little patterns, you intercept them, and you choose to make a change to how you're conditioned to behave in that moment. If you do that consistently enough and you keep practicing it, and you keep it up every day, then you're developing a new internal narrative through all those little actions, and it accumulates in ways that are pretty powerful. (00:55:43): Every now and then, there's things that you can do that are more of a brute force method of driving that home. Some may find it through a Vipassana retreat, a seven to 10-day silent retreat, which is agonizing if folks haven't tried to be that quiet that long. Things bubble up, you confront the stuff in your mind that in our day-to-day, it's easy to just keep it under the hood. Some find that through psychedelics. Some find that through somewhat extreme physical feats. (00:56:22): There was a period in time where I didn't realize this at the time, but not only was I building my career, but I was running ultra marathons. Looking back at that I was like, "Yeah, there I was, another desperate attempt to feel worthy," but I also recognize now that that was medicine for me, that me going out onto a remote mountain range for five hours every Saturday and just running well beyond the point of discomfort was consistently cathartic for me. I would cry at the end of almost every single one of those runs. So it's just a recap. It's in those little moments and sometimes in those big moments too, but it begins with the awareness based on truth and then the daily practice.
turns.zh: 对，这又回到了我之前提到的关于觉察——'好，我理解我有低自我价值感，我理解它以所有这些方式呈现出来，我对它有了觉察，现在当我在做一些是那个深层自我信念或负面核心信念所产生的 conditioned 行为或 conditioned 反应时，当我发现它，我就有一个干预的机会'——它从简单的方式开始。(00:54:31)：比如，我有过一个老板，他会过来一直给我表扬。他是个很棒的人，我觉得我做得不错。有一天他过来，说：'嘿，干得漂亮'，我的回应是：'哦，对，我尽力了'，然后他看着我说：'嘿，说谢谢或不客气。就这样。别人给你一个赞美，就说谢谢，接受它。'所以这成了我的一个模式——如果有人给我一个赞美，我看着他们的眼睛说'谢谢'，我真的努力 embrace 那个小瞬间，因为正是在所有这些方式中你识别出这些小模式、你拦截它们、你选择改变你在那个时刻被 conditioning 的行为方式。如果你足够一致地这样做、持续练习、每天坚持，那你就在通过所有那些小行动发展出一个新的内在叙事，它以相当强大的方式累积。(00:55:43)：偶尔有一些更 brute force 的方法可以把那个 driving home。有些人通过 Vipassana 闭关——7 到 10 天的静修——找到它，如果人们没试过那么长时间那么安静的话，那是极其痛苦的。东西会冒泡上来，你面对你脑子里那些在日常中很容易就压在台面下的东西。有些人通过迷幻剂找到。有些人通过某种极端的身体壮举找到。(00:56:22)：有一段时间——我那时候没意识到——我不只在建立我的职业生涯，我还在跑超级马拉松。回看那个我想：'对，我又一次为了感觉有价值的绝望尝试'，但我也现在认识到那对我来说是药，我每个周六去一个偏远的山脉跑五个小时、跑到远远超过不舒服的点，对我来说持续地是 cathartic 的。我几乎每次跑步结束都会哭。所以总结一下——它在那些小瞬间里，有时候也在那些大瞬间里，但它从基于真相的觉察开始，然后是日常练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long does this process often take for people that you've worked with?
turns.zh: 对于你合作过的人，这个过程通常需要多长时间？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: There are some famous figures that you can turn to. For example, Eckhart Tolle. He wrote The Power of Now, which he's probably most famous for. He's a great Western spiritual teacher of Eastern traditions. He went through immense suffering himself. Actually, the suffering was so great that for him it led to a somewhat sudden and spontaneous collapse of his sense of identity. Doctors would probably say psychosis, and what he actually had was a spiritual liberation, liberation from his mind, but he describes it himself. In reading his book and listening to some of his lectures and talking about his own journey, he wrote this at, I think, in the first chapter or the preface of The Power of Now when he described the suffering that he was experiencing and the sudden collapse of this sense of identity, and then waking up the next day and feeling this deep sense of peace and freedom for the first time in his life. (00:58:28): Then his journey continued to unfold. He eventually started to research to try and understand, "What had just happened to me? What experience did I have?" and dot, dot, dot. Seven years later, he woke up one day and realized he was now a spiritual teacher, seven years. It's not that the journey had ended, but to use a metaphor of two mountains and a valley, that first mountain in his life when he got off of that mountain and he entered this valley, between the first mountain of life and the second mountain of life, the valley that he was in that sat between the old sense of self and then this new sense of self as a spiritual teacher, that valley was seven years for him. (00:59:22): There are many other examples I can pull up like that, including Siddhartha Gautama, Lord Buddha himself. That wasn't a couple weeks or a couple of months, his journey towards liberation from his own mind. If I can recall, that was also a seven or eight-year journey. So these big shifts on a cosmic universal scale, it's instantaneous, right? On the scale of-
turns.zh: 有一些名人你可以参考。比如 Eckhart Tolle，他写了《当下的力量》，可能是他最著名的作品。他是一位伟大的西方精神导师，传授东方传统。他自己经历过巨大的痛苦。事实上痛苦大到对他来说导致了他身份感的某种突然和自发的崩溃。医生可能会说那是精神病，但他实际上经历的是精神解放——从他的心智中解放——但他自己描述。在读他的书和听他的一些讲座、谈他自己的旅程时，他在《当下的力量》的第一章或前言里写到——他描述了他正在经历的痛苦和这个身份感的突然崩溃，然后第二天醒来、人生中第一次感觉到这种深深的平静和自由。(00:58:28)：然后他的旅程继续展开。他最终开始研究试图理解：'我刚刚发生了什么？我经历了什么体验？'等等等等。七年之后，他有一天醒来意识到他现在是一个精神导师了——七年。不是旅程结束了，但用两座山和一个山谷的比喻，他人生中第一座山他下来、进入这个山谷——在第一座人生山和第二座人生山之间——那个位于旧的自我感和作为精神导师的新自我感之间的山谷，对他来说是七年。(00:59:22)：还有很多其他的例子我可以举，包括悉达多·乔达摩——佛陀本人。那不是几周或几个月，他走向从自己的心智中解放的旅程。如果我没记错，那也是七到八年的旅程。所以这些在宇宙尺度上的大转变是瞬间的，对吧？在……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:59:50] context.
turns.zh: （听不清）上下文。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah. On the scale of 13 billion years, it's instant, but from our perspective, it's not. It feels a lot longer than that.
turns.zh: 对。在 130 亿年的尺度上，它是瞬间的，但从我们的角度看不是。它感觉比那长得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to close the loop on these four steps that you shared, and the one we haven't talked about yet is the last one, which is building compassion towards others. How do you go about that just broadly? I know we're not going to solve that problem for people in the podcast.
turns.zh: 我想闭环你分享的这四个步骤，我们还没聊的是最后一个——建立对他人的同情。你大致怎么做到那个？我知道我们不会在播客里替人们解决那个问题。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: For me, my experience was that it happened automatically. When you do the first three, it is the result. It's the thing that comes out of step number three itself because, again, when you dig deep enough and you keep searching for the truth, you're like Captain Ahab going down with the white whale in Moby Dick. That is what that book is about. It's not about a fisherman going after a whale. This is the author himself through a story talking about his own journey of emotional and spiritual liberation. (01:00:57): There are many people that would, experts and historians that might disagree with that, and I would disagree with them that it's a story of seeking the truth at all costs to liberate oneself, including being willing to die for that whale, metaphorically, because at the end of the book, they don't really reveal. Did Ahab actually go down with the whale and never come back? Maybe he did, maybe he didn't. (01:01:27): So when you have suffered enough and the search for the truth becomes the only thing that matters and that truth leads you to understanding that, "It's okay. I can accept myself for who I am and it's not all my fault," when that has been done in earnest and when you feel those moments of love for yourself, it suddenly changes how you see everybody else. For me, step four was the easiest because it just happened. It happened after eight years, nine years of my own on and off mental health journey, but it finally happened.
turns.zh: 对我来说，我的经历是它自动发生了。当你做了前三个，它是结果。它是从第三步本身出来的东西，因为再说一次，当你挖得足够深、继续寻找真相，你就像 Captain Ahab 跟着白鲸一起沉下去的《白鲸记》。那本书讲的就是这个。它不是关于一个渔夫追一条鲸鱼。这是作者本人通过一个故事谈他自己的情感和精神解放之旅。(01:00:57)：很多专家和历史学家可能不同意那个，但我会不同意他们——它是一个不惜一切代价寻求真相以解放自己的故事，包括愿意为那条鲸鱼而死，比喻意义上的，因为在书的结尾，他们没有真正揭示。Ahab 真的跟鲸鱼一起沉下去再也没回来吗？也许他死了，也许他没有。(01:01:27)：所以当你受够了苦、寻找真相变成唯一重要的事、而那个真相引导你理解：'没关系，我可以接受自己本来的样子，这不全是我的错'——当那个被 earnestly 地做了、当你感受到那些爱自己的时刻，它突然改变了你看待其他所有人的方式。对我来说，第四步是最容易的，因为它就是发生了。它发生在我自己断断续续八九年的心理健康旅程之后，但它最终发生了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People who are listening to this say they're a VP of Product and they're like, "I don't want to become a spiritual teacher. I want to stay on this path. I want to have a successful career. I want to continue to make a bunch of money." How often do you find there's a path to stay on that path with a rejiggering of how you see the world or does it, if you're suffering enough, does it almost always lead to something completely different in your experience?
turns.zh: 听这个播客的人有些是产品 VP，他们会说'我不想成为精神导师，我想留在这条路上，我想有一个成功的职业，我想继续赚一大笔钱。'你发现有多大概率有这样一种路——在重新调整你看待世界的方式的同时留在这条路上？还是说如果你受够了苦，在你的经验里它几乎总是通向完全不同的东西？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Again, it's a spectrum. What I've experienced is that the vast majority of people who feel some tug to undergo a process of change, I'd say 90%, 95% of the time pretty confidently I can say that those changes are more of the micro transitions. It's, "Okay. Let me change my job. Let me downsize my house. Let me break up with my partner." Still hard things, and for them, that may be all that is needed and necessary. There's no moral judgment on my side about everyone's got to dive into the deep end. That's certainly not the case, and I'm not advocating for it. I honestly don't even know if it's a choice. There's a part of me that, based on some of the experiences I've had, believes that it was somewhat preordained and that this was going to happen for me, but it's in the minority of cases where the radical transformation of one's sense of identity takes place. It's not common. My general sense is it's definitely less than 1% of the population, and I suspect that's just the way things are.
turns.zh: 再说，它是一个光谱。我经历的是，绝大多数感到某种要经历改变过程的牵引的人——我可以说 90%、95% 的时候相当有信心——那些改变更多是微转化。就是：'好，让我换个工作，让我把房子换小，让我跟伴侣分手。'仍然是艰难的事，对他们来说那可能就是所需的、必要的。我对每个人都要一头扎进深水区没有道德评判。当然不是那样，我也不提倡。我甚至不知道这是不是一个选择。有一部分我，基于我有过的一些经历，相信这在某种程度上是注定的、这对我来说会发生。但身份认同的激进转变发生的 case 是少数。它不常见。我的总体感觉是它绝对低于人口的 1%，我怀疑事情就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of those ends up being Buddha, and one of those ends up being Andy Johns.
turns.zh: 其中一个最后成了佛陀，一个最后成了 Andy Johns。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah, or another popular figure in Western spirituality is Pema Chödrön, who she's got a lot of great books. One of them is titled When Things Fall Apart, some of the first books I read when things fell apart for me. Her story, actually, she used to live in Berkeley, I think, but an American woman. She was married. First marriage didn't work out. She got married again. Second one didn't work out. It ended in somewhat sudden and expected and catastrophic fashion. Here she is with a few children and a broken heart again and deep emotional suffering, and that suffering was so great that it led her to ultimately say, "I must pursue these teachings and this spiritual tradition that I'm starting to wake up to in the Eastern traditions," with Buddhism in particular because she had suffered so much that she needed to find liberation from that. (01:05:25): In her case, that even meant separating, not all the time, but a significant portion of her time away from her own children who, if I recall correctly, were early teens timeframe. Now, I think that Pema Chödrön is the only female Buddhist nun in all of North America and is a very well-known spiritual teacher. I also think her journey was somewhere around seven or eight years. Again, that's just the valley between two mountains. Truthfully, the journey continues for the rest of your life, but just another example I wanted to share.
turns.zh: 对，或者西方灵性里另一个受欢迎的人物是 Pema Chödrön，她有很多很棒的书。其中一本叫《When Things Fall Apart》，是我事情崩溃时读的最早的一些书。她的故事其实是——她以前住在伯克利，我想是一个美国女人。她结过婚，第一段婚姻没成，又结了，第二段也没成，以一种相当突然、expected（unexpected？）和灾难性的方式结束。她带着几个孩子、又一次心碎、深深的情感痛苦，那个痛苦大到让她最终说：'我必须追寻这些教诲和我开始觉醒的东方传统、特别是佛教'，因为她受了那么多苦，她需要从中找到解放。(01:05:25)：在她的 case 里，那甚至意味着分离——不是所有时间，但很大一部分时间——离开她自己的孩子，如果我没记错，那时候大概十几岁。现在，我认为 Pema Chödrön 是整个北美唯一的女性佛教比丘尼，是一位非常著名的精神导师。我也认为她的旅程大概七八年。再说，那只是两座山之间的山谷。truthfully，旅程持续你余生，只是另一个我想分享的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's some obvious reasons why going down this path is difficult, why making change is hard. What else would you say holds people back from making a big change in their life, and maybe on the flip side is just how do you allow change to happen?
turns.zh: 走这条路很明显很难，改变很难。还有什么你会说阻碍人们在生活中做出大改变，也许反过来就是怎么允许改变发生？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: A significant thing that holds people back from change is the inertia of civilization because we all experience a fundamental conflict in our life because when we're born, we have many needs, but there are two substantial needs that are immutable in everyone, especially children. The first need is the need for love, acceptance, and connection for mammals. We have one of the longest gestation periods of the entire animal kingdom, and even when we're born, we're helpless, we can't survive. We need nurturing for many, many more years afterwards in order to survive. (01:07:13): That goes hand-in-hand with our need for connection. So we're biologically hardwired to need to be accepted and connected because it is perhaps the most essential thing to survival, more essential than water. So we're born with that need. Yet at the same time, we're also born as unique individuals. (01:07:37): I read a study where the scientists estimated the probability that two sperm or two egg would be genetically identical. For context, I think the average man generates in their prime somewhere around between 10 to 100 million sperm a day. So we generate a lot of sperm in our lifetime. The math that they came up with was that the probability of two sperm being identical is roughly 10 to the 15th power, which is a million times greater than the number of stars in the Milky Way galaxy. There's somewhere between 100 to 400 billion stars in the galaxy. So it's a million times greater than that. So all that is to say is when you were born, you were unique. There's never been a you before ever, and it's going to be a really, really long time or another dimension before another one of you shows up again. (01:08:32): Then further through the socialization of life, we all have unique experiences, and those experiences are passed through this unique prism of our own mind and genetics to where we're further accentuated as individuals. So we're born with this fundamental need to be connected and to be loved, but we're also born with this need to be ourselves and to express ourselves. What ends up happening though is the world that you're born into eventually conditions you away from the unique individual that you were, and that is the function of society. (01:09:09): Society operates because enough people choose to agree on the same beliefs and ideas around the style of education, of raising children, of city planning, of millions of things. So the substrate of society or the adhesive of it is shared belief. So that's why I say the inertia of civilization or I should have said the inertia of society is because you're born into a world that begins to condition you at a very early age to act a certain way and not act a certain way, believe some things and don't believe others. (01:09:48): Why am I a San Francisco Giants fan? Well, because I grew up in a Giants family. It's not like I was two years old and I picked the Giants. It doesn't work that way. What ends up happening then is, and this begins, again, really young. You're two, three, four, five years old and the world around you, namely the adults in the world, start telling you who to be, and it begins to challenge or run into conflict with that individuality, but because our fear of not being accepted and loved is so great that what do we end up doing? We choose to push down our individuality in exchange for being accepted by the pack, beginning with our parents, and then our friends, and then our teachers, and then our bosses, and all of the other dimensions of society. (01:10:42): So we lose who we were before the world told us who to be. It's actually a Carl Jung quote, "The world will ask you who you are, and if you don't know, it'll tell you." So I would say that that is the number one reason why transformation doesn't take place. It's because a long time ago, we made that exchange to forego our individuality in order to be accepted by others because of that deep primal need for love and acceptance. In order to undertake that process of personal transformation, one of the truths you have to realize is that truth, that truth that you are in large part the way you are but because of what the world told you to be, and it's making the choice consciously to then say, "Fuck that, and I'm going to go against the grain and I'm going to now tell the world that I don't want its influence on me anymore, and I will, like Moby Dick or like Ahab going down with the white whale, I am willing to die to return to my individuality and to break free and to be who I want to be in the face of the currents around us regarding the messages around how we should think, live, act, and feel." (01:12:11): So that is the thing that prevents transformation. The simple thing is you could say fear, but what is the fear? That is the fear. It's to say, "I'm going to walk my own path now and I'm going to be who I want to be, and I'm going to discover who I was before the world told me who to be, and by doing so, I run the risk that I'm not going to be accepted anymore." That's terrifying.
turns.zh: 一个阻碍人们改变的 important 的东西是文明的惯性，因为我们都在生活里经历一个根本的冲突——我们出生时有很多需要，但有两个 substantial 的、每个人尤其是孩子不可改变的需要。第一个是对爱、接纳和连接的需要。哺乳动物有整个动物王国最长的孕期之一，即使出生了，我们是无助的，我们没法生存。我们需要很多很多年的 nurturing 才能生存。(01:07:13)：这跟我们对连接的需要 hand in hand。所以我们在生物学上被 hardwired 去需要被接纳和连接，因为那也许是生存最本质的东西，比水还本质。所以我们生来就有那个需要。但同时，我们也生来作为独特的个体。(01:07:37)：我读过一项研究，科学家估计两个精子或两个卵子基因完全相同的概率。作为背景，我觉得男人在 prime 时期每天产生大约 1000 万到 1 亿个精子。所以我们一辈子产生很多精子。他们算出来的数学是，两个精子相同的概率大约是 10 的 15 次方，比银河系里恒星的数量多一百万倍。银河系里大约有 1000 亿到 4000 亿颗恒星。所以比那多一百万倍。所以这一切都是说，当你出生时，你是独特的。从来没有过你，将来要很长很长时间或另一个维度才会有另一个你出现。(01:08:32)：然后通过生活的社会化，我们都有独特的经历，那些经历通过我们独特的心智和基因的 prism 被传递，以至于我们作为个体被进一步 accentuated。所以我们生来有这个被连接和被爱的根本需要，但我们也生来有做自己、表达自己的需要。但最终发生的是，你出生的世界最终把你从你本来的独特个体 conditioning 开，那是社会的功能。(01:09:09)：社会运作是因为足够多的人选择在相同的信念和理念上达成一致——关于教育方式、养育孩子、城市规划、百万件事情。所以社会的 substrate 或黏合剂是共享信念。这就是为什么我说文明的惯性——或我应该说的是社会的惯性——是因为你出生在一个很早就开始 conditioning 你以某种方式行动、不某种方式行动、相信一些事、不相信其他事的世界。(01:09:48)：为什么我是旧金山巨人队的球迷？嗯，因为我在一个巨人队家庭长大。不是我两岁的时候自己选了巨人队。不是那样运作的。那么最终发生的是——这又开始了，真的很小，你两三四五岁，你周围的世界，也就是世界里的大人，开始告诉你该成为谁，它开始挑战或跟那个个体性冲突，但因为我们不被接纳和不被爱的恐惧如此之大，我们最终做什么？我们选择压下我们的个体性以换取被群体接纳——从我们的父母开始，然后我们的朋友，然后我们的老师，然后我们的老板，以及社会的所有其他维度。(01:10:42)：所以我们失去了在世界告诉我们该成为谁之前的那个我们。这其实是 Carl Jung 的话：'世界会问你是谁，如果你不知道，它会告诉你。'所以我会说这是转变不发生的头号原因。是因为很久以前，我们做了那个交换——放弃我们的个体性以换取被他人接纳——因为那种对爱和接纳的深层原始需要。要 undertake 那个个人转化的过程，你必须意识到的真相之一是——那个真相：你很大程度上是你这样，是因为世界告诉你要成为什么——然后有意识地做出选择说：'去他妈的，我要逆流而上，我现在要告诉世界我不要再它的影响了，我会像 Moby Dick 或像 Ahab 跟着白鲸沉下去那样，我愿意为了回到我的个体性、为了挣脱、为了成为我想成为的人而死，面对围绕我们的、关于我们应该怎么想、怎么活、怎么行动、怎么感受的潮流。'(01:12:11)：所以那才是阻止转变的东西。简单的答案你可以说恐惧，但恐惧是什么？那就是恐惧。就是说：'我现在要走我自己的路，我要成为我想成为的人，我要发现世界告诉我该成为谁之前的那个我，这样做我冒着不再被接纳的风险。'那太可怕了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because it's so terrifying, I imagine that's why the suffering is so important to really feel that because, otherwise, why would you go down that path? It feels very hard.
turns.zh: 因为太可怕了，我猜这就是为什么痛苦如此重要、要真正感受到那个，因为不然你为什么会走那条路？感觉太难了。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah, and that gets to my point earlier around I'm not entirely convinced that this is an act of free will on my part. There have been moments of me intervening and acting with free will, but I believe that there are also undercurrents that would fall into the realm of superstition for a lot of folks that this is the path that was laid out in front of me even before I was born.
turns.zh: 对，这跟我之前的点联系起来——我不完全相信这是我自由意志的 act。有过我干预、以自由意志行事的时刻，但我相信也有一些 undercurrents——对很多人来说会落入迷信的范畴——这是在我出生之前就 laid out 在我面前的路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those same lines, you wrote in one of your writings that at the end of the day, you're on your own to find what ends up alleviating your psychological suffering. Can you speak to that?
turns.zh: 就着同样的思路，你在你的一篇写作里写到，归根结底你要靠自己找到什么能缓解你的心理痛苦。你能讲讲那个吗？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah. That really ties in with this point of the uniqueness of people. You have to find what works for you. For some people, it's going to be the ice bath thing. For others it's not. Last year, a quick anecdote, I spent a month working at an animal sanctuary in northern Thailand for abused animals and neglected animals. This place is amazing. They take in anything and they say, "We'll find a way," and that's what they do. So they have hundreds and hundreds of animals, including a large herd of elephants, which is pretty amazing. (01:14:24): There was a worker there who I met, and just by the expression on his face, I could tell that this was a liberated man. This was somebody who had figured out something that was contributing to his deep sense of peace. So I went to talk with him. I said, "Hey, something tells me that you figured out the secret to life and I'd like to chat." So we talked, and it turned out that half the time he was a farmer, he had a small little farm, an acre up on a hill in the mountains, and he'd work at his farm half the time and the other half he would then go and work at the animal sanctuary, and he was a practicing Buddhist. (01:15:15): One of the things he said to me really stood out. He used a simple analogy. He said, "Everyone's trying to make it to Bangkok. The problem is they're getting to Bangkok by following somebody else's road. The whole point is to find your own path to Bangkok." He was making that same point or a similar point of you've got to find your own way. That is the message. For me, I take that as maybe the most fundamental message in looking back at the story of the original Buddha himself was, sure, the teachings, the traditions, everything that's formed around his teachings has power and merit to it, but I look at what he did. He was born as a prince into a royal family. Something wasn't right, and he was seeking the truth behind this anguish and this unfulfillment, and there was something inside of him that said, "I must seek the answer because growing up in this sheltered life as a prince, this can't be the answer." (01:16:31): So he left it all behind, including his wife and child, and then he lived as an aesthetic for years, nearly dying close to starvation. He did that for years. Then eventually he realized, "Well, that's not the answer either." Then he famously made his way to the Bodhi tree and sat under it and meditated for 40, 41 days. I can't recall what it was, a long time. Then he had his enlightenment, and out of that came one of the teachings, which is known as the middle way. It's not about being a prince, it's not about being poor. There's something in between. He found that was his path to Bangkok. You could walk that path and maybe it'll teach you something or it'll lead you nowhere because it's not your own path. I think that's the point.
turns.zh: 对。这真的跟人们独特性这一点联系在一起。你必须找到对你有效的。对有些人，会是冰浴那套。对其他人不是。去年，一个小故事，我在泰国北部一个动物保护区工作了一个月，那里是给被虐待和被忽视的动物的。这个地方太棒了，他们什么动物都收，说：'我们会找到办法'，他们就是那样做的。所以他们有几百只动物，包括一大群大象，相当 amazing。(01:14:24)：那里有一个工作人员，我遇到他，光从他的脸上我就能看出这是一个被解放了的人。这是一个搞明白了某种东西、正在贡献给他深深平静感的人。于是我找他聊。我说：'嘿，有什么告诉我你搞明白了生活的秘密，我想聊聊。'我们聊了，原来他一半时间是个农民，他在山上有一小块一英亩的农场，一半时间在自己农场干活，另一半时间去动物保护区工作，他是个修行的佛教徒。(01:15:15)：他跟我说的有一句话很突出。他用了一个简单的比喻，他说：'每个人都想去曼谷。问题是他们走别人的路去曼谷。重点是找到你自己的去曼谷的路。'他在讲同样的点或类似的——你得找到你自己的路。那就是信息。对我来说，我把那个当作也许是最根本的信息——回看原始佛陀本人的故事：当然，教诲、传统、围绕他的教诲形成的一切都有力量和价值，但我看他做了什么。他生为王子，在皇室家庭。有什么不对劲，他在寻求这个痛苦和不满足背后的真相，他内心有某种东西说：'我必须寻求答案，因为在这样被 sheltered 的王子生活里长大，这不可能是答案。'(01:16:31)：所以他抛下一切，包括妻子和孩子，然后作为苦行者生活了好几年，几乎饿死。他那样做了好几年。然后最终他意识到：'嗯，那也不是答案。'然后他著名地走到了菩提树下，冥想了 40、41 天，我记不清是哪个，很长时间。然后他有了他的 enlightenment，从中出来的一个教诲叫'中道'。不是关于做王子，不是关于做穷人，有什么在中间。他找到了那是他的去曼谷的路。你可以走那条路，也许它会教你什么，也许它哪儿也不通，因为不是你自己的路。我觉得那才是点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Andy, what a beautiful way to wrap up our conversation. Before we do, is there anything else you want to share that you want to leave listeners with? Then also, I'm just curious how you're doing these days.
turns.zh: Andy，这是结束我们对话的美好方式。在我们结束之前，还有什么你想分享的、想留给听众的吗？然后我也好奇你这些天怎么样。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Sure, sure. Well, let me answer the first one, a message to leave to folks. I would imagine that there's a lot of high performers, successful folks out there. Some of you, you may feel like you're on the verge of answering a call towards a new chapter in life or towards finding a way out of whatever situation you're in that you don't want to be in anymore. The thing I guess I would say to you is that having undergone some change myself, all I can promise you is that it's going to be in some ways the best thing that's ever happened to you, but also the worst thing that's ever happened to you, but those are the experiences that define a life. (01:18:36): If you feel that call inside of you to seek a new way of living, just know that you're not the only one out there doing it. There are others out there such as myself and that I can always be reached. So I wish you a happy journey and just know that things are going to be okay. Now, the second question, what am I up to nowadays? Is that-
turns.zh: 好的，好的。让我回答第一个，给 folks 的信息。我想有很多高成就者、成功人士。你们中有些人，你们可能感觉自己正处于回应一个 call、进入人生新篇章或找到走出你不想要的处境的边缘。我猜我想对你说的是，我自己经历过一些改变，我能 promise 你的只是，它在某些方面会是你人生中最好的事，但也是最糟的事，但那些才是定义一生的经历。(01:18:36)：如果你内心感觉到那个 call、要寻找一种新的生活方式，只要知道你不是唯一一个在做这件事的人。有其他人比如我，我总是可以被联系到。所以我祝你旅途愉快，只要知道事情会没事的。现在第二个问题，我这些天在做什么？是那个——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How are you doing? How are you doing on this journey?
turns.zh: 你怎么样？你在这条旅程上怎么样？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: I'm good. I still have my ups and downs. I've arrived at an interesting part in my journey where it's something that I'm practicing now and I still don't quite have the hang of it. I'll use one more metaphor. I think the way that I approached the first part of my life was as if life was a big mountain to be climbed, where you're trying to head up Everest under this assumption that once you get to the top, you're going to have this bliss that will persist or that will make you feel that you had a life well-lived, and that that was the answer, but what I experienced was that once I got to the top of one mountain, then I had to find the top of another and another and another. Although you see and do some amazing things along the way, at some point it's too exhausting. At some point, you may really get yourself into trouble and you might not survive. (01:20:13): The vast majority of people who die on Mount Everest actually die on the way down, not on the way up. You don't save anything for the return home, I think is the point. Instead of pursuing my life now as a mountain to be climbed in the hopes that reaching the top will make me feel good again, I'm instead trying to float down river. So for example, if you go whitewater rafting, they'll give you a little safety crash course at the beginning. They'll say, "Here's how you paddle. Put your vest on." One of the things they'll ask you is, what do I do if I fall overboard, especially if I fall overboard into the rapids or the cold water? This is maybe the most important thing they teach because commonly what happens if you're in sizable enough rapids and you fall overboard, the tendency is to freak out and to fight the current. When people freak out in the water, especially when the water's choppy, that's when they get in trouble. (01:21:20): The thing they teach you to do is instead you go into mummy mode, right? You lay back, you cross your arms across your chest, and you stick your feet out like you're a mummy, and you do the opposite of fighting the current. You allow the current to take you where it's trying to take you. For me, I actually find that I believe that that's a more fitting metaphor for life. It's possible that there's something amazing for us downstream so long as we're willing to surrender and just let go, to turn off the intellectual mind a bit, to quit trying to plan as if you can predict the future, to quit thinking about all the edge cases and trying to optimize our life, which I think is a bunch of bullshit. It's possible that if you just relax and you instead pay attention to the signals around you, you feel where the current is trying to take you, maybe towards a potential life partner, maybe away from an oppressive work environment, maybe towards a place to live that is more calm and peaceful, whatever it may be. (01:22:33): If you really tune in with yourself and pay attention to that current and you relax into it, you'll arrive at a destination that you were meant for. In a sense, that's what I did that has brought me to this conversation today. Instead of talking about investing in companies and what have you, I'm instead trying to connect with people on an entirely different level and help them make their own way downstream, so to speak. (01:23:11): So for me nowadays, that's how I'm living at the moment. I'm actually in Vietnam. Just got here about 10 days ago because it seemed like the current of life was taking me here right now. It's likely that it's just the next lily pad towards wherever else I'm heading to, but I guess I'm in the mindset now where I'm willing to just surrender and see how it unfolds.
turns.zh: 我很好。我还是有起有落。我到了我旅程里一个有趣的部分，它现在是我正在练习的某件事，我还是没完全掌握。我再用一个比喻。我觉得我前半生对待生活的方式，就好像生活是一座要爬的大山，你在试图上珠穆朗玛峰，假设一旦你到顶，你就会有这种会持续的 bliss 或会让你觉得你度过了 well-lived 的一生、那就是答案。但我经历的是，一旦我到了一座山的山顶，然后我得找另一座的顶、又一所、又一座。虽然沿途你看到和做一些 amazing 的事情，到某个点它太令人疲惫了。到某个点你可能真的让自己陷入麻烦，你可能活不下来。(01:20:13)：死在珠穆朗玛峰上的人绝大多数其实死在下山的路上，不是上山的路上。你不为回家留任何东西，我想这是 point。我现在不再把生活当作一座要爬的山、希望到顶能让我重新感觉好，我而是在试着顺河而下。比如，如果你去白水漂流，他们会一开始给你一个小安全课。他们会说：'这是怎么划桨，穿上你的救生衣。'他们会问你的一件事是：如果我掉下水了怎么办，特别是如果我掉进急流或冷水里怎么办？这也许是他们教的最重要的事，因为通常如果你在足够大的急流里掉下水，tendency 是 freak out、对抗水流。当人们在水里 freak out，特别是当水 choppy 的时候，那就是他们出事的时候。(01:21:20)：他们教你做的是相反——你进入 mummy mode，对吧？你躺回去，双臂交叉在胸前，脚伸直像一个木乃伊，你做的是跟对抗水流相反的事。你允许水流把你带去它要带你去的方向。对我来说，我其实发现我相信那是一个更 fitting 的生活比喻。可能下游有什么 amazing 的东西在等我们，只要我们愿意 surrender、就放手，把智识心智关掉一点，quit 试图预测未来一样做计划，quit 思考所有 edge cases、试图优化我们的生活——我觉得那是一堆 bullshit。可能如果你就放松、然后注意你周围的信号，你感觉水流在试图把你带去哪里——也许朝向一个潜在的人生伴侣，也许远离一个压抑的工作环境，也许朝向一个更平静、更 peaceful 的居住地——无论是什么。(01:22:33)：如果你真的 tune in 自己、注意那个水流、你 relax 进去，你会到达一个你 meant for 的目的地。在某种意义上，这就是我做的、它把我带到了今天的这次对话。不是谈投资公司之类的，我而是在试图在一个完全不同的层面上与人连接、帮助他们以自己的方式 downstream。所以比喻上。(01:23:11)：所以对我来说现在，那就是我当下的生活方式。我其实在越南。大概 10 天前刚到，因为看起来生活的 current 现在把我带到这里。它很可能只是下一个 lily pad、通往我接下来要去的任何地方，但我想我现在在这样一个 mindset 里——我愿意就 surrender、看它怎么展开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The metaphor for that is they lost your luggage on the way to Vietnam, and we had to push back this recording a week.
turns.zh: 这个比喻就是他们在去越南的路上把你的行李弄丢了，然后我们不得不把这次录音推迟了一周。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Yeah, that's right, that's right. My luggage was half a world away from me, and so when that happened, what could I do? I just said, "Okay. Well, I have shorts and a shirt on me that I can wear for the next three or four days," and that's what I did.
turns.zh: 对，没错，没错。我的行李在半个地球之外，所以当那件事发生的时候，我能做什么？我就说：'好，我有身上穿的短裤和 T 恤，可以穿三四天'，那就是我做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Andy, I think this might end up being one of the most meaningful episodes of the podcast. I think it's going to end up being a Trojan horse for people are coming here for advice on optimizing their product and growth, and they'll opt up rethinking their whole life, hopefully in a good way, maybe cause some suffering, maybe help people through suffering. Thank you, Andy, so much for being here. Two final questions. You said people could reach out if they're going down this path and maybe need some help or advice. So what's the best way for people to reach out, and then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Andy，我觉得这可能会成为这个播客最有意义的几期之一。我觉得它会成为一个特洛伊木马——人们来这里是为了获取优化产品和增长的建议，但会不小心重新思考他们整个人生，希望是以一种好的方式，也许引发一些痛苦，也许帮人们度过痛苦。Andy，非常感谢你来。最后两个问题。你说人们如果走这条路、也许需要一些帮助或建议，可以联系你。人们联系你最好的方式是什么？然后听众怎么能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Sure, a couple ways. You can find me on Twitter, my username is Clues Dot Life, so C-L-U-E-S-D-O-T-L-I-F-E. You can also find me on LinkedIn, search for Andrew Johns, you'll find me on there. You can check out my website Clues.Life. It's a basic MVP, but it's an art project that's in process. So those are a couple of ways that you can reach out. In terms of ways you can help, you can't always tell who you're helping. When I sit behind my laptop and I write and I send my messages out into the world, other than getting some thumbs up here and there, you don't always know what impact you're having. (01:25:22): Sometimes it's good to hear because, again, for me, this is part of me rewriting that internal narrative where I'm trying to do more work for the benefit of others as opposed to what it does for my bank account. So if part of this message has been beneficial to you, it would certainly put wind in my sails to hear that. So that would be one way to help.
turns.zh: 好的，几种方式。你可以在 Twitter 找到我，我的用户名是 Clues Dot Life，C-L-U-E-S-D-O-T-L-I-F-E。你也可以在 LinkedIn 找我，搜 Andrew Johns，你能找到我。你可以看我的网站 Clues.Life。它是一个基本的 MVP，但这是一个进行中的艺术项目。所以这些是你可以联系到我的几种方式。关于你可以怎么帮忙——你没法总是知道你在帮谁。当我坐在笔记本后面写东西、把我的信息发到世界上，除了偶尔得到一些点赞，你不总是知道你在产生什么影响。(01:25:22)：有时候听到反馈是好的，因为再说一次，对我来说，这是我重写内在叙事的一部分——我在试图做更多为他人利益的工作，而不是为我的银行账户做什么。所以如果这个信息的一部分对你有益，听到那个肯定会给我 wind in my sails。所以那是一种帮忙的方式。

turns.en: What a great answer. So let's blow up the YouTube comments and send you some DMs and LinkedIn messages if people find this valuable. Andy, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 多好的回答。所以各位，如果觉得有价值，让我们把 YouTube 评论区炸了、给你发些 DM 和 LinkedIn 消息。Andy，再次非常感谢你来。

turns.speaker: Andy Johns
turns.en: Lenny, I appreciate it, man. Thank you.
